title: Water Distribution Overview for Operators
audience: Operators and trainees across the US and Canada preparing for certification exams and renewal in water distribution work.
prerequisites: Basic arithmetic and a calculator. Familiarity with the Basic Hydraulics course helps with the foundation calculations. US customary units are primary with metric equivalents; all scenarios and system data are fictional. Treatment-plant and wastewater topics are not covered.
introduction: Build a working picture of a drinking-water distribution system: its components and layout, how it is operated through the day, what maintenance, repair, meters and backflow protection involve, and how water quality, customer contact and compliance awareness fit in. Each module has worked examples and quick checks that name common mistakes. Safety content is recognition and purpose only, and facility procedures govern.
delivery: Self-paced lessons, optional quick checks, a graded final exam and a non-credit certificate. Duration is being validated; no contact-hour award is made.

modules.title: System components and layout
objectives: Trace water from source to tap and name the job of each component, including pump stations, storage, mains, valves, hydrants, service lines and meters.
Compare tank types and state what storage does for demand, fire flow, pressure and water age.
Explain pressure zones, branched versus grid layouts and dead ends, and how common pipe materials tend to fail and corrode.
modules.lesson: ### What a distribution system is for A distribution system is everything between the treatment plant (or a well) and the customer's tap: pumps, storage tanks, mains, valves, hydrants, service lines and meters. Treatment makes the water safe; distribution has to keep it safe while delivering the right amount at a usable pressure, day and night, and holding a reserve for fire fighting. Contaminated water moving through pipes has spread waterborne disease, so a distribution operator protects public health every day. The pipe network is part of the treatment barrier, not just plumbing. In the figure, treated water is lifted by a pump station into a main that passes an elevated tank, a valve and a hydrant. A service line then leaves the main and passes a meter on its way to the customer. Every component moves, stores, controls or measures water. ### Storage: why tanks exist Storage does four jobs. It **equalises demand** by filling when use is low and supplying water when use is high, so pumps and the plant can run steadily. It holds a **fire-flow reserve**, because a fire can demand far more water for a few hours than customers use in a whole afternoon. It **stabilises pressure**, because the water level in a tank sets the pressure around it. It also gives an **emergency supply** during a power loss. Tank level follows the demand cycle. When customer use is below the pumped rate the tank fills; when use is above it the tank drains. A healthy elevated tank therefore rises and falls over a day, and a tank that never moves may be a sign of a closed valve or a stuck control. ### Tank types and how each works - **Clear well:** a treated-water basin at the plant that gives contact time and a buffer for the high-service pumps. It sits at the plant, not out in the system. - **Elevated tank:** the water column provides pressure by gravity. Each foot of water height gives **0.433 psi** (about 9.8 kPa per metre). - **Standpipe:** a tall cylinder on the ground. Only the upper part of the water column gives useful pressure, so the lower water is "dead storage" that pumps must lift unless the standpipe is drained. - **Ground storage tank:** water is stored at ground level and re-pumped into the system. It holds large volumes cheaply but gives no pressure of its own. - **Hydropneumatic tank:** a sealed steel vessel where compressed air holds the water under pressure; pumps start and stop on pressure. If the air cushion is lost to absorption or leaks, the tank becomes "waterlogged" and the pump **short cycles**, starting and stopping rapidly and wearing out. The air-to-water ratio matters, and the design sets it. - **Surge tank:** a vessel near a pump or at a high point that supplies or absorbs water during a sudden pressure change. Its role against surge is limited; it eases some events but does not replace good valve operation. ### Worked example: pressure from a tank level *Alder Bend is fictional. A hydrant gauge sits 118 ft below the water surface in an elevated tank. Use 0.433 psi per foot.* **Step 1:** pressure = height x 0.433 = 118 x 0.433 = **51.1 psi** (about 352 kPa). **Step 2:** the tank drops 12 ft during the evening peak: 12 x 0.433 = **5.2 psi** less at the gauge, so about 45.9 psi. Friction loss in the pipes lowers the real pressure further while water is flowing. The hydraulics course covers that. ### Water age in tanks Water spends time in a tank, and the longer it sits the more disinfectant it loses, the more it warms, and the more taste, odour and bacteria problems can develop. A tank that fills and draws only a small slice of its volume each day holds old water. This is why tanks are **covered**, screened and vented, why they have hatches that lock, and why they must be **accessible for inspection and cleaning**. Module 4 returns to water age as a customer-facing problem. ### Pressure zones and minimum pressure Ground elevations vary, so one pressure cannot suit a whole town. Customers in a valley would see damaging pressure while customers on a hill would see almost none. A **pressure zone** is an area fed from its own tank, pump station or pressure-reducing valve so that pressure stays within a workable range. Boundary valves between zones are normally closed or are one-way controls. The reason for a **minimum pressure** is public health as much as comfort. If pressure falls toward zero, outside water can be drawn into the pipe through leaks and connections. The applicable rule or utility standard sets the number; this course does not. Utilities also try to keep pressure from becoming excessive, since high pressure stresses pipes, fittings and household plumbing. ### Fire protection and storage design The **ISO fire-protection grading** rates a community's water supply, fire department and alarm system. A better grade can lower insurance cost for residents and businesses, so the utility has a financial reason to keep adequate mains, hydrants and storage. The design engineer and fire authority set the required fire flow. ### Pipe materials and how they fail - **Gray cast iron:** old, brittle and rigid, often with lead or bell-and-spigot joints. It tends to crack across the barrel (circumferential breaks) or split lengthwise after a shock or ground movement. - **Ductile iron:** replaced cast iron because it can bend slightly before it breaks. Push-on and mechanical joints are common. Its main enemy is corrosion, especially in aggressive soil. - **Steel:** used for large mains, with coatings and linings to protect it and welded or flanged joints. Coating damage leads to corrosion. - **Asbestos cement (AC):** installed in earlier decades. The concern is for the worker: cutting, drilling or sanding releases fibres into the air, so the employer's written work practices and regulations apply. Aggressive water can also soften the pipe wall. - **PVC:** a common plastic pipe, light, easy to handle and corrosion resistant. It has a pressure class marked on it, can be weakened by long sunlight exposure, and can sag or fail if bedding and backfill are poor. - **Concrete:** large-diameter mains in two main types, prestressed and embedded cylinder. Failure usually starts with a corroding steel wire or cylinder inside the wall. - **HDPE:** flexible and fused or joined with fittings, often used for crossings and trenchless installation. - **Lead service lines:** older small lines to the customer. They are an awareness issue, covered in Module 4. **Selection factors** include pressure, soil, corrosion risk, joint type, diameter, cost and the utility's experience. ### Corrosion and electrical issues Corrosion is an electrical process. A metal pipe in wet soil develops anodic areas, where metal dissolves, and cathodic areas, where it does not. Different metals, soil types and stray currents all drive it. Protection includes coatings, **polyethylene encasement** of iron pipe, and **cathodic protection**, where a **sacrificial anode** (a more active metal) corrodes in place of the pipe, or a **rectifier** supplies a controlled direct current. Where joints are rubber-gasketed, **bonding** or electrical continuity across joints may be added to make protection work. **Service pipes must not be used as the electrical ground** for household wiring: current on the water line speeds corrosion and is a shock hazard to anyone who cuts into it. ### Layouts and reading the map A **branched (tree) layout** sends water down one path to each customer. The ends are **dead ends**, where water ages and sediment settles, and a single break cuts off everyone downstream. A **loop** returns the line to a second connection, and a **grid** interconnects many loops, so water has more than one route. Grids give the best redundancy and fire flow, and they allow isolating a break while keeping most customers in service. A **distribution map** shows pipe size, material, installation year, valves, hydrants, zone boundaries and service connections. Operators use it to plan which valves isolate a section and which customers are affected.

### Fictional scenario: the Alder Bend extension

Alder Bend is a fictional town that is adding a street to the end of an old branched main. The main is 1950s gray cast iron, and the town's only elevated tank sits 118 ft above the new street's hydrant. A supervisor asks whether to extend the dead end or to loop the new street back to a second main, and what pressure the new customers can expect when the tank is full.

### Your decision

Calculate the static pressure from the tank level, name one risk of leaving a dead end, and say what you would check about the old pipe before tying in.
modules.assignment: Write a half-page note for the Alder Bend supervisor. Calculate the static pressure from 118 ft of water using 0.433 psi per foot, explain in your own words why a loop is better than a dead end, and list two checks about the existing pipe. Do not state a required pressure; say the applicable rule or utility standard sets it.
rubric: Calculates 118 x 0.433 = 51.1 psi and notes that friction lowers real pressure while water flows.
Explains that a dead end holds old water and a single break cuts off everyone downstream, while a loop gives two paths.
Names sensible checks such as pipe material and condition, tie-in valves and the utility standard, without quoting a limit.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Static pressure = 118 x 0.433 = 51.1 psi (about 352 kPa). Accept answers that mention water age, sediment and loss of service at a dead end and the redundancy of a loop. Good checks include confirming the old main's material and condition, joint type, valve locations on the map and any asbestos-cement work practices. Do not accept a required minimum pressure from the learner as a limit; the applicable rule or utility standard sets it.

checks.prompt: Fictional Alder Bend uses its elevated tank to keep pumps running steadily. The main storage purpose that lets the pumps do this is:
choices: Raising the chlorine residual in the water as it sits in the tank
Replacing the need for any disinfection or treatment at the plant
Filling at low demand and supplying water at high demand
Lowering the pressure that customers in the zone experience
checks.explanation: Equalising demand lets pumps run near a steady rate while the tank covers the peaks. The "Raising the chlorine residual in the water as it sits in the tank" choice is wrong because a residual falls with time in a tank. The "Replacing the need for any disinfection or treatment at the plant" choice confuses storage with treatment, which still has to happen first. The "Lowering the pressure that customers in the zone experience" choice has the effect reversed, since tank level sets the pressure around it.

checks.prompt: A fictional service gauge sits 74 ft below the water surface in an elevated tank. Use 0.433 psi per foot of water. The static pressure at the gauge, to one decimal place, is:
choices: 32.0 psi
74.0 psi
46.7 psi
checks.explanation: Pressure = height x 0.433 = 74 x 0.433 = 32.04, or 32.0 psi. The "170.9 psi" choice multiplied by 2.31 feet per psi instead of dividing. The "74.0 psi" choice read the 74 feet as 74 psi without converting. The "46.7 psi" choice added 14.7 psi of atmospheric pressure, which gives absolute pressure instead of the gauge pressure asked for.

checks.prompt: A fictional hydropneumatic tank has lost its air cushion, and its pump now starts and stops rapidly. This condition is best described as:
choices: A surge tank absorbing a pressure wave
A clear well that is running too full
An altitude valve that has closed on a full tank
A waterlogged tank causing short cycling
checks.explanation: A hydropneumatic tank needs a cushion of compressed air to hold pressure between pump starts; without it the pump short cycles. The "A surge tank absorbing a pressure wave" choice names a different vessel with a different job. The "A clear well that is running too full" choice describes a treatment-plant basin, not a pressure vessel. The "An altitude valve that has closed on a full tank" choice describes a valve that protects an elevated tank from overflow, not a cause of rapid pump starts.

checks.prompt: A fictional town extends a branched main with a dead end serving one street. A main break upstream of that street will most likely:
choices: Leave the street supplied through a second path
Cut off supply downstream of the break
Raise the residual at the dead end of the main
Be isolated without any loss of service
checks.explanation: In a branched layout each customer has one path, so a break upstream removes supply downstream. The "Leave the street supplied through a second path" choice describes a loop or grid, which the street does not have. The "Raise the residual at the dead end of the main" choice reverses the effect, since dead ends are where residual is lost. The "Be isolated without any loss of service" choice assumes redundancy that a tree does not give.

checks.prompt: A fictional utility bonds a sacrificial magnesium anode to a buried steel main. The purpose of the anode is to:
choices: Carry the household electrical ground for nearby buildings
Corrode in place of the pipe so the pipe is protected
Slow the water so that sediment can settle out
Replace the coating that the pipe would have needed
checks.explanation: A sacrificial anode is a more active metal that gives up its material first, protecting the steel. The "Carry the household electrical ground for nearby buildings" choice repeats the unsafe practice of using the water system as an electrical ground. The "Slow the water so that sediment can settle out" choice describes a settling basin, not corrosion control. The "Replace the coating that the pipe would have needed" choice treats the anode as a coating; it works alongside a coating.

checks.prompt: A fictional crew will cut and drill into an old asbestos-cement main. The main concern in the work plan is that this work:
choices: Adds asbestos to the drinking water inside the pipe
Makes the pipe lose pressure class at once
Contaminates the water with lead from the joints
Releases fibres into air the worker could breathe
checks.explanation: The recognised hazard of asbestos-cement pipe is airborne fibre from cutting, drilling or sanding, so written work practices govern. The "Adds asbestos to the drinking water inside the pipe" choice treats it as a water-quality issue rather than a worker hazard. The "Makes the pipe lose pressure class at once" choice invents an immediate strength loss. The "Contaminates the water with lead from the joints" choice mixes in lead, which belongs to old service lines and joints rather than this pipe.

modules.title: Operating the system
objectives: Describe daily demand patterns and how a tank floats on the system.
Apply tank draw-down, velocity and main-volume calculations and cross-refer to the hydraulics course for theory.
Recognise valve types, valve exercising, water hammer, hydrant types and parts, and the purpose of flushing and flow testing.
modules.lesson: ### Demand patterns through the day Customers do not use water evenly. Use is lowest in the small hours, climbs to a **morning peak** as people wake, dips through the middle of the day, and rises to an **evening peak**. Summer lawn watering, a holiday, a heat wave or a large industrial user can reshape the curve. Peaks that last only an hour or two are why a system needs storage: pumps and the treatment plant are sized and run for something close to the average, and tanks cover the difference. ### How tanks float on the system A tank connected to the distribution system by a single pipe "floats on the line." Its water level is set by the pressure in the system: when pumps push harder than the tank's head, water flows in and the level rises; when demand pulls pressure down below the tank's head, the tank flows out and the level falls. In the figure, the tank level rises overnight when demand is below average and falls through both peaks. Operators often use tank level to start and stop pumps, so a failed level sensor can empty or overflow a tank. Tanks that fill and drain through separate pipes mix water better, which helps against water age. ### Foundation calculations (the hydraulics course has the theory) These are the four calculations a distribution operator uses most. For the reasoning behind head, friction and flow, use the Basic Hydraulics course; here we only apply it. **1. Pressure from elevation.** Pressure in psi = height of water in feet x 0.433 (or height / 2.31). It is the same calculation as Module 1. **2. Tank fill and draw-down.** Volume = area x depth x 7.48 gal per ft3, with area = 3.1416 x diameter squared / 4. *Worked example. The Kestrel Ridge tank is fictional: a 40 ft diameter cylinder whose level falls 6 ft over the evening peak.* **Step 1:** area = 3.1416 x 40 x 40 / 4 = **1,256.6 ft2**. **Step 2:** volume = 1,256.6 x 6 = 7,539.8 ft3. **Step 3:** gallons = 7,539.8 x 7.48 = **56,398 gal** (about 213,000 L). Divide by the net outflow in gpm to estimate how long a draw-down takes. **3. Velocity in a main.** Velocity = flow (cfs) / area (ft2), and 1 cfs = 449 gpm. *Worked example. A fictional 8 in main carries 600 gpm.* **Step 1:** area = 3.1416 x (8/12)2 / 4 = 3.1416 x 0.4444 / 4 = **0.3491 ft2**. **Step 2:** flow = 600 / 449 = **1.336 cfs**. **Step 3:** velocity = 1.336 / 0.3491 = **3.83 ft/s**. The design engineer or utility standard sets any limit; the value is for judging whether a flushing or fire flow is stressing the main. **4. Volume of a main.** Gallons = area x length x 7.48. Operators use it to estimate how much water a flushing or a repair involves. The hydraulics course lists the full set of unit conversions. ### Valves: types and purposes - **Gate valve:** meant to be fully open or fully closed. A rising-stem gate valve shows its position by the stem height; a non-rising stem needs a turn count. Throttling a gate valve damages the gate. - **Butterfly valve:** a disc that stays in the flow even when open. It is compact and used on larger mains. - **Check valve:** allows flow in one direction and closes against reverse flow. Its closure can cause surge if it slams. - **Pressure reducing valve (PRV):** holds a lower pressure downstream. Its **downstream setting** decides what customers in the lower zone feel, so it is a real operating setting, not a casual adjustment. - **Altitude valve:** a diaphragm-operated valve at a tank that closes when the tank is full so it will not overflow, and opens when pressure falls. - **Air release valve:** vents trapped air at high points. Entrapped air acts like a partly closed valve and cuts flow. ### Water hammer and valve operation **Water hammer** is the pressure spike caused by a sudden change in water velocity. Slamming a valve, stopping a pump or a check valve closing hard can all cause it. Pressure waves can break pipes, blow gaskets and damage fittings. The purpose of operating valves slowly is to let velocity change gradually. Closure times belong to the utility's procedure and the engineer. **Valve exercising** means operating each valve through its range on a schedule. Its purpose is to keep valves from seizing, to find ones that are stuck, buried or the wrong way round, and to keep the map accurate. A valve found stuck during exercising costs far less than a valve found stuck during a main break. ### Hydrants: types and parts A **fire hydrant** gives fire crews water and gives operators a way to flush and test. - **Dry-barrel hydrant:** the main valve is at the base, below the frost line, and the barrel above holds no water when the hydrant is closed. A drain port empties the barrel after use. This design suits freezing climates. The operating nut at the top turns the stem that opens the base valve. - **Wet-barrel hydrant:** the barrel stays full, with a valve at each outlet. It suits mild climates because standing water can freeze and split the barrel. Below grade, a **lateral** connects the hydrant to the main, with an **isolation valve** so the hydrant can be shut off for repair without taking the main out of service. A **thrust block** or restraint keeps the pressure from pushing the hydrant off its connection. Lateral size is a design matter: it must pass the fire flow. **Flush hydrants** are low, often flush with the pavement, at airports and bridges where a tall hydrant would be a hazard. ### Colour classes, operation principles and records Many utilities paint hydrant bonnets or caps by capacity class. The colour tells fire crews the **rated flow class** of the hydrant, which helps them decide how many are needed; the class meaning is set by the utility's or fire authority's standard. The principles of operation, at recognition level: a hydrant is designed to be run **fully open or fully closed**, because a partly open dry-barrel hydrant may not drain properly and can scour. It should be closed slowly and not forced beyond the stop. Utilities remove or leave off caps as their procedures state. Follow the facility's written procedure for any actual operation, which includes protecting people and property from the discharge. A hydrant taken out of service should be **marked** so fire crews do not rely on it. Inspection and maintenance records, with dates, findings and repairs, show the utility's care and help plan replacement. Lubricants, paints and other materials that touch drinking water must be **certified to the drinking-water contact standard** the regulator recognises. A good general-purpose grease is not an acceptable substitute. ### Flushing programs and flow tests A **flushing program** moves water at higher velocity through selected mains to carry out sediment, rust and old water, and to restore a disinfectant residual. It follows a plan: which mains, in what order, with the water sent safely to drain, and with customers told ahead of time if discoloration is likely. A **flow test** measures a hydrant's flow and the pressure drop on a nearby hydrant, to show what the main can deliver for fire fighting. The fire-protection standard for hydrant flow testing sets the method. Test results support fire-flow planning, ISO grading and finding closed valves or tuberculated pipe that cut capacity.

### Fictional scenario: the Kestrel Ridge evening peak

Kestrel Ridge is a fictional town whose 30 ft diameter tank falls by 4.5 ft every summer evening. A crew plans to flush a stretch of 10 in main at 900 gpm and wants to know how much water the tank loses and how fast the water will move. A hydrant on the route also looks seized.

### Your decision

Find the tank volume drawn in one evening and the main velocity during flushing. Say which valve and hydrant checks you would make first and how you would record them.
modules.assignment: Write a half-page plan for the Kestrel Ridge crew. Calculate the gallons drawn from the tank and the velocity in the 10 in main, state which constants you used, and describe the purpose of exercising valves and testing the hydrant. Do not give closure times or limits; say the utility procedure sets them.
rubric: Calculates the tank volume with area x depth x 7.48 and the velocity with flow in cfs divided by area.
States the purpose of valve exercising and hydrant inspection and records what was found.
Avoids stating closing times, minimum flows or limits and refers to the utility procedure.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Tank volume = 3.1416 x 30 x 30 / 4 = 706.9 ft2; x 4.5 ft = 3,181 ft3; x 7.48 = 23,794 gal. Velocity = (900 / 449) / (3.1416 x (10/12)2 / 4) = 2.004 / 0.5454 = 3.67 ft/s. Accept answers that name valve exercising as a way to find stuck valves and note that the seized hydrant should be marked out of service and reported. Do not accept a closing time or velocity limit from the learner as a rule.

checks.prompt: At fictional Marrow Creek the elevated tank level rises overnight and falls through the evening peak. This pattern most directly shows that the tank:
choices: Floats on the system, rising and falling with its pressure
Is held at one level by a closed valve on its inlet pipe
Is cut off from the pressure of the zone it serves
Is raised and lowered by readings at customer meters
checks.explanation: A tank on a single line follows system pressure, so its level tracks the demand cycle. The "Is held at one level by a closed valve on its inlet pipe" choice would show a level that does not move. The "Is cut off from the pressure of the zone it serves" choice would also leave the level flat, since it would not see system pressure. The "Is raised and lowered by readings at customer meters" choice treats customers as the control, although pumps and valves respond to the tank.

checks.prompt: A fictional 20 ft diameter ground tank is being checked. Use 3.1416 for pi and 7.48 gal per ft3. The gallons held in each foot of depth, to the nearest gallon, are:
choices: 314 gal
checks.explanation: Area = 3.1416 x 20 x 20 / 4 = 314.2 ft2, and 314.2 x 7.48 = 2,350 gal per foot of depth. The "9,400 gal" choice forgot to divide by 4. The "314 gal" choice stopped at square feet. The "141,058 gal" choice used 449 gpm per cfs in place of 7.48 gal per ft3.

checks.prompt: A fictional technician sees a rising-stem gate valve with its stem standing fully extended above the bonnet. That position indicates the valve is:
choices: Closed, because the stem has backed out of the bonnet
Partly throttled, which is its normal duty
Failed, because stems should not move
Open, because the gate has lifted clear of the flow
checks.explanation: On a rising-stem gate valve a high stem shows the gate lifted, so the valve is open. The "Closed, because the stem has backed out of the bonnet" choice reverses the stem position. The "Partly throttled, which is its normal duty" choice is wrong because gate valves are meant to be fully open or fully closed, and throttling can damage the gate. The "Failed, because stems should not move" choice ignores that the stem is supposed to rise and fall.

checks.prompt: A fictional village in a cold climate chooses a hydrant that keeps no water in the barrel when closed. This type is the:
choices: Wet-barrel hydrant, with a separate valve at each outlet
Dry-barrel hydrant, with its valve below frost depth
Flush hydrant, with its outlet set at pavement level
Altitude hydrant, with a diaphragm valve at the nozzle
checks.explanation: A dry-barrel hydrant drains the barrel above its base valve, which suits freezing weather. The "Wet-barrel hydrant, with a separate valve at each outlet" choice keeps the barrel full and suits mild climates. The "Flush hydrant, with its outlet set at pavement level" choice is about placement, for airports and bridges, not frost protection. The "Altitude hydrant, with a diaphragm valve at the nozzle" choice mixes up an altitude valve, which protects tanks, with hydrants.

checks.prompt: A fictional crew exercises line valves on a schedule. The main purpose of valve exercising is to:
choices: Raise the pressure in the zone for a short time
Replace the need for any hydrant flushing program
Keep valves from seizing and confirm they work
Reduce the chance of any water hammer to zero
checks.explanation: Exercising finds stuck, buried or mislocated valves before an emergency. The "Raise the pressure in the zone for a short time" choice is not an effect of operating a valve. The "Replace the need for any hydrant flushing program" choice confuses two separate maintenance tasks. The "Reduce the chance of any water hammer to zero" choice overstates it, and slow operation is what limits surge.

checks.prompt: A fictional crew finds an air-binding problem at a high point in a long main, where trapped air cuts flow like a partly closed valve. The valve that is meant to vent that air is the:
choices: Air release valve
Altitude valve
Pressure reducing valve
Check valve
checks.explanation: An air release valve sits at high points and vents entrapped air. The "Altitude valve" choice protects an elevated tank from overflow. The "Pressure reducing valve" choice holds a lower downstream pressure. The "Check valve" choice stops reverse flow and does not vent air.

modules.title: Maintenance and repair awareness
objectives: Name common causes of main breaks and leaks and recognise common leak detection methods.
Explain the purpose of disinfecting repaired mains, and describe service connections, meter types and meter accuracy.
Recognise cross-connections, backsiphonage and backpressure, and match backflow assemblies to the hazard.
modules.lesson: ### Main breaks and leaks: causes Pipes fail for a mix of reasons that act together. **Corrosion** thins the wall of iron and steel. **Ground movement**, freezing and thawing, and dry or wet soil cycles load the pipe from outside. **Pressure surges** and water hammer add sudden stress. **Traffic loads**, nearby digging, poor bedding and **poor joints** concentrate the stress. **Age and material** matter too: brittle old cast iron tends to snap across, while a corroded ductile or steel main tends to pit through. Seeing the failure type (circumferential break, longitudinal split, joint leak, pinhole) helps the engineer find the cause and prevent a repeat. ### Leak detection at recognition level Many leaks never reach the surface, so utilities look for them. Common approaches are **acoustic listening**, where sensors on valves and hydrants pick up the sound of escaping water; **correlators**, which compare that sound at two points to place a leak between them; **tracer gas** for plastic pipe where sound travels poorly; **district metering**, where a small zone's night-time flow is watched for a rise; and a review of **unexplained pressure drops** or customer reports. The purpose is to find losses early, save treated water and energy, and reduce the chance of a catastrophic break. *Worked example. A fictional leak at Pike Hollow runs at 2.5 gpm and goes unnoticed for 30 days. Use 1,440 min per day.* **Step 1:** minutes = 1,440 x 30 = 43,200 min. **Step 2:** loss = 2.5 x 43,200 = **108,000 gal** of treated water, from a leak too small to see on the surface. That is why small, steady leaks add up. ### Main repair and disinfection of repaired mains, concept level A repair has two jobs: restore the pipe, and keep the water in the system safe. When a main is open to the trench, dirt and groundwater can enter. The concept is to **isolate** the section with valves, keep the trench as clean as practical, use clean and properly stored materials, and **disinfect, flush and verify** before the line is returned to service. The utility's procedure and the applicable standard set the method and dose, and sample results decide whether the line can be released. A broken main may also have lost pressure, so nearby customers may need a notice about the water. This course does not teach the steps; follow the written procedure and the supervisor. ### Service connections and meters A **service connection** includes the tap on the main, a **corporation stop**, the service line, a **curb stop**, and a **meter**. The utility usually owns the line to the curb stop or meter, and the customer owns the rest. The material and size are set by the utility standard. Some older service lines are **lead**, which is why a service-line inventory is part of lead awareness. **Why meters exist:** to bill fairly, to spot customer-side leaks, and to track demand so the utility can plan. **Meter types:** - **Positive displacement (piston, nutating disc):** water fills and empties a chamber of known size. Accurate at low flows, common in homes, but it adds head loss and wears over time. - **Velocity meters (propeller, multi-jet):** the speed of a rotor reflects flow velocity. - **Turbine:** a rotor in a pipe spool for large flows, used for large commercial customers and master meters. - **Compound:** two chambers, one for low flows and one for high flows, so a single meter reads both well. - **Venturi, orifice, proportional:** differential-pressure devices with a restricted throat. Air entrained in the water disturbs the reading. - **Magnetic:** electrodes read a voltage made by water moving through a magnetic field. There are no moving parts, but the pipe must be full. - **Ultrasonic:** transducers send sound pulses through the water, and the difference in **transit time** between directions gives velocity. Meters can be read by hand, by **AMR** (a radio-read device a vehicle passes) or by **AMI** (a fixed network sending near real-time data, which also helps find leaks). Meter accuracy drifts down with wear, so utilities run a **testing and replacement program**. Large meters are tested more often because the volume at stake is higher, and the interval is set by the utility or its standard. *Worked example. Fictional meter at the Linden Court plant: a test passes a known 50.0 gal and the meter registers 47.0 gal.* **Step 1:** accuracy = 47.0 / 50.0 = **94 percent**. **Step 2:** the meter has recorded 7,520 gal this quarter. True use = recorded / accuracy = 7,520 / 0.94 = **8,000 gal**. The customer was under-billed by 480 gal. A slow meter loses revenue and hides leaks. ### Cross-connections and backflow A **cross-connection** is any link between drinking water and something that could contaminate it: a hose in a bucket of chemical, a boiler loop, an irrigation system, a fire sprinkler with additives. **Backflow** is flow in the wrong direction. A **pollutant** affects quality or appearance but is not a health threat; a **contaminant** is a health hazard. The hazard rating decides how strong a device is needed. A customer who only waters a lawn is a lower hazard than a plant that mixes chemicals, so the two get different protection. There are two causes. **Backsiphonage** happens when supply pressure drops (a main break, heavy fire flow) and the pipe acts like a straw. **Backpressure** happens when the customer's system pressure exceeds the supply pressure, as with a pump or boiler. ### Backflow assemblies at recognition level - **Air gap:** a physical open space between the outlet and the possible contamination. It is the most effective protection because nothing can be drawn across it. - **Reduced pressure zone (RPZ) assembly:** two checks with a relief port between them; the pressure in the middle zone is kept lower than the supply, so if a check fails, water is vented rather than flowing back. It is the best mechanical device for high-hazard use. - **Double check assembly:** two checks in a row, suitable for low-hazard protection but not for high hazard. A **residential dual check** is a smaller version for home service lines. - **Atmospheric vacuum breaker:** an air inlet that opens when supply pressure falls. It protects against backsiphonage only, at a fixture with no continuous pressure downstream. - **Pressure vacuum breaker:** a spring-loaded version that handles backsiphonage but not backpressure. **Containment** puts the protection at the meter or property line and protects the whole system from that customer. **Isolation** puts it at the specific fixture. A utility may require both. Assemblies are checked by a **qualified tester** on a regular schedule, because checks and springs foul or wear out without any outward sign. The rule and utility program set the schedule and the reporting. ### Inspection, records and trench safety Records are part of the job: valve exercising logs, hydrant inspections, main break reports, leak survey results, meter tests and backflow test reports. Good records show who did what, when and what was found, and they feed replacement planning and regulatory reports. Trench and traffic safety is recognition only here. A trench can collapse with no warning, so utilities must follow excavation rules: protective systems and a competent person who inspects the excavation. Excavators need utility locates, atmospheric checks for confined spaces where needed, and traffic control to protect crew and the public. The facility's safety program and the rules that apply govern these jobs.

objectives: Explain why a disinfectant residual is kept and where water age causes problems.

modules.lesson:
### Why a disinfectant residual is kept

Treatment kills or inactivates most microbes, but the pipe network is long, has joints and tanks, and can be disturbed by breaks and repairs. A **disinfectant residual** is a small amount of disinfectant left in the water as it leaves the plant. It keeps working in the pipes, helps control regrowth, and acts as an early warning: a residual that drops sharply between two points tells the operator something is using it up, such as old water, a biofilm or a contamination event. The applicable rule or permit sets the required residual; this course does not. Operators measure it at routine points and record it. Field measurement uses a test kit or colorimeter used exactly as the method directs, with fresh reagents, a clean sample cell, a calibrated instrument and a result read right away, because chlorine changes in a sample bottle. Record the value, time, location, test method, sample temperature and who took it. A residual that suddenly reads zero at a normally steady point deserves a repeat reading and a call to the supervisor before anything is assumed. Equally, an unexpectedly high reading may point to an instrument problem or a feed problem upstream, so confirm it before reporting a change.

### Water age and where it causes problems

**Water age** is the time since water left treatment. It grows in oversized mains, dead ends, low-use areas and tanks that barely turn over. Problems that follow include a falling residual, warmer water, and more taste and odour complaints, and in some systems more disinfection by-products or nitrification. Operators respond with flushing, adjusting tank cycling, looping dead ends where possible, and adjusting valves.

*Worked example. The Willow Mill tank is fictional: it holds 500,000 gal and, on average, 125,000 gal passes through it each day.*

**Step 1:** water age is roughly volume / daily flow.

**Step 2:** 500,000 / 125,000 = **4.0 days**. If a quarter of the volume is dead storage that never mixes, the working volume is smaller, but the stagnant part can be much older than the average.

*Worked example: residual loss along a main. At the fictional Heron Flats system, free chlorine leaving the plant reads 1.60 mg/L and the last tap on a dead-end main reads 0.40 mg/L.*

**Step 1:** loss = 1.60 - 0.40 = 1.20 mg/L.

**Step 2:** percent lost = 1.20 / 1.60 x 100 = **75 percent**. The number is not a pass or fail by itself. It points the operator toward the stretch of main to flush or loop, and the permit still sets the minimum that must be held.

### Customer complaints: taste, odour, colour and pressure

A complaint is useful data. A field operator should respond politely, record it, check it and report it. The record should include the date and time, the address, the caller's contact details, what was noticed, whether it is hot water, cold water or both, and what the operator found. Common patterns are:

- **Taste or odour:** often old water, low residual, a recently changed source or a plumbing problem inside the building. Check the residual at the tap and nearby hydrants. A chlorine smell can mean fresh water, not a problem.
- **Colour (brown or red):** usually iron stirred up by a flow reversal, a hydrant use or a break. Yellow, white or cloudy water may be air, sediment or other causes. Flushing usually clears it. Note which direction the flow reversed.
- **Low pressure:** check whether it is one house (inside plumbing, a closed curb stop, a clogged meter strainer) or the neighbourhood (a main break, a closed valve, a pump or tank problem). Compare with nearby customers.
- **High pressure or hammer:** may signal a PRV problem or a quick valve closure.

If the pattern suggests a health concern, such as sudden illness reports or an evident contamination, the operator escalates to the supervisor and follows the system's emergency plan. Records of complaints let the utility see clusters and trends that no single call shows.

*Worked example. Over one week the fictional Cedar Rise zone, with 1,200 customers, logs 18 brown-water calls.* Complaint rate = 18 / 1,200 x 1,000 = **15 calls per 1,000 customers**. If the call log shows the addresses clustered on two streets within a day of hydrant flushing, the likely cause is stirred-up sediment, and a short follow-up flush with a recorded residual check is a sensible response. If the calls are scattered across the zone with no event nearby, look wider: a source change, a tank problem or an old main.

### Coliform sampling: purpose and site idea

Coliform bacteria are **indicators**. They are not usually the cause of illness themselves, but their presence suggests that contamination might have reached the water, so a positive result triggers an investigation and repeat sampling. The applicable rule sets how many samples, how often and the response. The utility's **sample siting plan** picks representative locations across the system, including dead ends and areas with low residual, not just easy ones. A sample tap should be clean and representative of the mains water, and the sample must be collected using the lab's method and kept at the right temperature, since poor technique can create a false result. Records of the sample, time, residual and location go with the sample to the lab.

### Lead and copper at concept level

Lead and copper enter water mostly from the **plumbing** after the main: lead service lines, lead solder, brass fixtures and copper pipe. Water that is more corrosive dissolves more of these metals, especially after it sits in the pipe. Systems therefore use **corrosion control** treatment and sampling at the tap of higher-risk homes. A **service-line inventory** identifies which lines are lead, galvanized or unknown. The rule sets sampling, action levels and replacement duties. Operators should know that a main repair or meter replacement can disturb a lead line, so the utility's procedures and customer notices apply.

### Public notification

**Public notification** is the duty to tell customers when something affects their water, from a contamination event or treatment failure to a violation. Its purpose is to let people protect themselves, and the rule sets who has to be told, how quickly and in what words. An operator's role is to report promptly and accurately and to leave the wording to the person responsible. A customer-facing message should use plain language, say what happened, what to do and who to call.

### Operator certification and continuing education

Operators are certified because the work affects public health. Exams test the knowledge in this course at the entry level, and higher grades are required for larger or more complex systems. **Continuing education** keeps the operator current with rules, equipment and safety methods, and is usually required for renewal. The certifying agency sets the hours and the renewal cycle. This course is a non-credit learning pilot and does not award CEUs or contact hours.

### Working with the regulator and the public

The regulator is a partner as much as an inspector. Operators should keep accurate records, answer questions plainly, report problems early, and ask when unsure. With the public, being clear, polite and consistent builds trust: explain what the utility is doing, why, and how long it will take. Do not guess or speculate about health effects; refer questions to the person responsible. Plain, early honesty is better than a polished answer that turns out to be wrong.

### Fictional scenario: Willow Mill and Cedar Rise

Willow Mill is a fictional system with a 450,000 gal tank that passes about 180,000 gal each day. At the dead end of its Cedar Rise zone, which has 1,600 customers, the residual reads 0.45 mg/L against 1.80 mg/L leaving the plant, and 24 brown-water calls arrived in one week.

### Your decision

Find the tank's water age, the percent of residual lost and the complaint rate. Say what you would flush or sample and what you would tell customers.
modules.assignment: Write a half-page response for the Willow Mill supervisor. Calculate the water age, the residual loss and the complaint rate per 1,000 customers, and explain in your own words how you would respond, record and communicate. Do not state a required residual; say the applicable rule or permit sets it.
rubric: Calculates water age 450,000 / 180,000 = 2.5 days, loss 75 percent and rate 15 per 1,000.
Proposes a measured response such as flushing the dead end, rechecking the residual and recording the calls and results.
Uses plain customer language and refers to the rule or permit for any required residual or notice without quoting a limit.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Water age = 450,000 / 180,000 = 2.5 days. Residual loss = (1.80 - 0.45) / 1.80 = 75 percent. Complaint rate = 24 / 1,600 x 1,000 = 15 per 1,000. Accept plans to flush or loop the dead end, check tank turnover, sample representative sites and log each call. Do not accept a stated minimum residual as a limit; the applicable rule or permit sets it.

Read the source sections and note one point that applies to your own system.
Work through the case evidence and prepare the written assignment.
Compare one answer with a distractor mistake, then self-check against the case evidence. Optional notes can capture your reasoning; count only active work.

checks.prompt: A fictional operator asks why a small disinfectant residual is kept in the pipes after treatment. The best reason is that the residual:
choices: Keeps working in the pipes and warns when it is used up
Replaces the need for flushing the distribution system
Improves taste by lowering the water temperature
Raises the pH to protect the pipe from corrosion
checks.explanation: A residual protects against regrowth and warns of old water or contamination. The "Replaces the need for flushing the distribution system" choice is not a substitute for flushing. The "Improves taste by lowering the water temperature" choice is unrelated to residual. The "Raises the pH to protect the pipe from corrosion" choice mixes the residual with corrosion control.

checks.prompt: The fictional Cedar Rise zone has 1,600 customers and logs 24 brown-water calls in a week. The complaint rate per 1,000 customers is:
choices: 1.5 calls per 1,000
15 calls per 1,000
67 calls per 1,000
0.015 calls per 1,000
checks.explanation: Rate = 24 / 1,600 x 1,000 = 15 calls per 1,000 customers. The "1.5 calls per 1,000" choice multiplied by 100, which gives a percent. The "67 calls per 1,000" choice inverted the ratio. The "0.015 calls per 1,000" choice stopped before multiplying by 1,000.

checks.prompt: A fictional lab reports coliform bacteria in a routine sample. The way to understand this result is that coliform:
choices: Is the usual cause of most waterborne illness in pipes
Is expected in treated water at low background levels
Is a measure of the disinfectant residual in the pipe
Is an indicator that contamination may have arrived
checks.explanation: Coliform is an indicator, so a positive result triggers repeat sampling and investigation. The "Is the usual cause of most waterborne illness in pipes" choice overstates it. The "Is expected in treated water at low background levels" choice dismisses a result the rule treats as a signal. The "Is a measure of the disinfectant residual in the pipe" choice confuses a bacterial test with a chemical residual.

checks.prompt: Brown water appears on two fictional streets a day after hydrant flushing. The most likely cause is:
choices: Iron and sediment stirred up by changed flow
A very high chlorine residual in the system
A failed meter at each of the affected homes
Lead dissolving from the nearby water tower
checks.explanation: Flushing or flow reversals can lift deposits, so the colour is iron and sediment. The "A very high chlorine residual in the system" choice would not colour the water. The "A failed meter at each of the affected homes" choice would affect one home, not a street. The "Lead dissolving from the nearby water tower" choice mixes in a metal that comes from plumbing.

checks.prompt: A fictional utility explains that most lead in tap water comes from:
choices: The treatment plant clear well and its transfer pumps
Plumbing after the main, like service lines and solder
The natural water in the river or aquifer source
The hydrant lateral running under the street
checks.explanation: Lead mostly enters from service lines, solder and fixtures, especially after water sits. The "The treatment plant clear well and its transfer pumps" choice is not a source of lead. The "The natural water in the river or aquifer source" choice is not typical. The "The hydrant lateral running under the street" choice is public piping that does not feed taps.

checks.prompt: A fictional contamination event affects a neighbourhood. The purpose of public notification is to:
choices: Replace the need for reports to the regulator on events
Assign blame to the operator nearest to the event
Let customers protect themselves with plain, timely facts
Reduce the number of calls that customers make
checks.explanation: Notification exists so people can protect their health, and the rule sets who is told and when. The "Replace the need for reports to the regulator on events" choice is a separate duty. The "Assign blame to the operator nearest to the event" choice is not a purpose. The "Reduce the number of calls that customers make" choice may happen, but it is not the reason.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional tank at Kestrel Ridge has a water surface at elevation 640 ft. A customer's service is at elevation 512 ft. Use 0.433 psi per foot of water and 2.31 ft per psi. Ignoring friction, the static pressure at the customer, to one decimal place, is:
choices: 55.4 psi
finalAssessment.explanation: Static head is the elevation difference, 640 - 512 = 128 ft, and 128 x 0.433 = 55.42, or 55.4 psi. The "277.1 psi" choice used the tank elevation alone instead of the difference. The "295.7 psi" choice multiplied by 2.31 feet per psi instead of dividing. The "221.7 psi" choice used the customer's elevation alone.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional standpipe level falls from 62 ft to 49 ft above a pressure gauge at its base. Use 0.433 psi per foot of water. The drop in static pressure at that gauge, to one decimal place, is:
choices: 5.6 psi
30.0 psi
26.8 psi
21.2 psi
finalAssessment.explanation: The change in head is 62 - 49 = 13 ft, and 13 x 0.433 = 5.63, or 5.6 psi. The "30.0 psi" choice multiplied the drop by 2.31 instead of dividing. The "26.8 psi" choice converted the starting level instead of the change. The "21.2 psi" choice converted the ending level instead of the change.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional standpipe holds water from its floor up to its overflow. A pump must lift the water that lies below the height needed for minimum pressure, which is called:
choices: Fire-flow reserve, which no pump is allowed to touch
Surge storage, which is sized to absorb water hammer
Clear well volume, which is kept for contact time
Dead storage, which gives no useful pressure on its own
finalAssessment.explanation: In a standpipe the lower water cannot give acceptable pressure, so it is dead storage unless pumped. The "Fire-flow reserve, which no pump is allowed to touch" choice is a planned reserve at usable height, not the unusable lower water. The "Surge storage, which is sized to absorb water hammer" choice confuses storage with a surge vessel. The "Clear well volume, which is kept for contact time" choice names a plant basin.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional hillside neighbourhood sees very high pressure while a ridge top sees very low pressure from the same main. The usual remedy that also protects pipes and fixtures is to:
choices: Close the boundary valve and leave the ridge top dry
Create separate pressure zones with a PRV or tank
Add a larger check valve at the treatment plant
Raise the whole system until the ridge has enough
finalAssessment.explanation: Zones are fed from their own tank, pump or reducing valve so each stays in a workable range. The "Close the boundary valve and leave the ridge top dry" choice leaves customers without service. The "Add a larger check valve at the treatment plant" choice treats a check valve as a pressure control, which it is not. The "Raise the whole system until the ridge has enough" choice would push valley pressures higher and stress pipes and plumbing.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional utility lists the pipe it holds as old gray cast iron, ductile iron and PVC. Compared with gray cast iron, ductile iron is valued because it:
choices: Is immune to corrosion even in aggressive soil
Can bend slightly before it breaks, resisting shock
Is light enough to need no thrust restraint
Comes with a pressure class marked on each joint
finalAssessment.explanation: Ductile iron has the strength of iron with some flexibility, which cast iron lacks. The "Is immune to corrosion even in aggressive soil" choice is wrong because ductile iron still corrodes and often needs encasement. The "Is light enough to need no thrust restraint" choice ignores that thrust restraint is needed at bends and ends for most pressure pipe. The "Comes with a pressure class marked on each joint" choice borrows a marking feature of PVC.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional tank at Kestrel Ridge is a 30 ft diameter cylinder, and its level falls 4.5 ft over the evening peak. Use 3.1416 for pi and 7.48 gal per ft3. The volume drawn from the tank, to the nearest gallon, is:
choices: 425 gal
finalAssessment.explanation: Area = 3.1416 x 30 x 30 / 4 = 706.9 ft2; volume = 706.9 x 4.5 = 3,180.9 ft3; gallons = 3,180.9 x 7.48 = 23,793. The "95,172 gal" choice forgot to divide the area by 4. The "3,181 gal" choice stayed in cubic feet. The "425 gal" choice divided by 7.48.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional 10 in main carries 900 gpm. Use 3.1416 for pi, 449 gpm per cfs and velocity = flow in cfs divided by area in ft2. The velocity in the main, to two decimal places, is:
finalAssessment.explanation: Area = 3.1416 x (10/12)2 / 4 = 0.5454 ft2; flow = 900 / 449 = 2.004 cfs; velocity = 2.004 / 0.5454 = 3.68 ft/s. The "0.92 ft/s" choice forgot to divide the area by 4. The "1,650.11 ft/s" choice used gpm without converting to cfs. The "220.60 ft/s" choice divided by 7.48 instead of 449.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional water hammer event follows a hard hydrant closure. The most direct cause of a hammer wave is:
choices: A slow rise in the chlorine residual at the plant
A tank that is nearly empty at the evening peak
A sudden change in the speed of moving water
A hydrant that was left with its cap on tightly
finalAssessment.explanation: Water hammer comes from a sudden velocity change, which is why valves are operated slowly. The "A slow rise in the chlorine residual at the plant" choice has no hydraulic effect on pressure. The "A tank that is nearly empty at the evening peak" choice would lower pressure, not make a spike. The "A hydrant that was left with its cap on tightly" choice has no bearing on a closure.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional fire captain asks what the colour on a hydrant bonnet tells her crew. The best answer is that it:
choices: Shows that the hydrant has been taken out of service
Gives the pipe material of the hydrant lateral
Records the date of the last valve exercise on the main
Marks the rated flow class the utility assigned
finalAssessment.explanation: Many utilities paint by capacity class so crews know what flow to expect. The "Shows that the hydrant has been taken out of service" choice is done with a separate marking such as a bag or tag. The "Gives the pipe material of the hydrant lateral" choice is not what colour is used for. The "Records the date of the last valve exercise on the main" choice would be a record entry, not a paint colour.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional technician wants a grease for a hydrant stem that will touch drinking water. The suitable product is one that:
choices: Is a general-purpose grease taken from the shop shelf
Is certified for drinking-water contact by a standard
Is labelled as weather resistant and long lasting
Is the thickest and stickiest grease on the shelf
finalAssessment.explanation: Materials touching drinking water must be certified for that use. The "Is a general-purpose grease taken from the shop shelf" choice is a common but unsafe habit. The "Is labelled as weather resistant and long lasting" choice describes performance, not safety for water contact. The "Is the thickest and stickiest grease on the shelf" choice treats thickness as a measure of suitability.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional customer meter has tested at 93 percent accuracy, meaning it registers 93 percent of the water that passes. It recorded 14,880 gal in a quarter. The actual use, in gallons, is:
finalAssessment.explanation: True use = recorded / accuracy = 14,880 / 0.93 = 16,000 gal. The "13,838 gal" choice multiplied by 0.93, which lowers the figure again. The "15,922 gal" choice added 7 percent of the recorded value, which is not the same as dividing. The "1,042 gal" choice found the lost fraction of the recorded value, not the true use.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional plant uses a chemical that is harmful at low concentration, and the utility must choose a device at the meter. The best choice for a high-hazard connection is:
choices: A reduced pressure zone assembly
A residential dual check valve
A double check assembly
An atmospheric vacuum breaker
finalAssessment.explanation: An RPZ is the strongest mechanical device and is used for high hazard. The "A residential dual check valve" choice is a light-duty device for homes. The "A double check assembly" choice is suited to low hazard. The "An atmospheric vacuum breaker" choice protects against backsiphonage only and is not meant for continuous pressure.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional irrigation system has a pump that can raise downstream pressure above the supply. A fictional installer proposes a pressure vacuum breaker. The concern is that this device:
choices: Handles backsiphonage but not backpressure
Needs a power supply to hold its checks closed
Is the same as an air gap in effectiveness
Fails open whenever supply pressure is high
finalAssessment.explanation: A pressure vacuum breaker uses an air inlet for backsiphonage and does not handle back pressure. The "Needs a power supply to hold its checks closed" choice invents a power need. The "Is the same as an air gap in effectiveness" choice overstates its protection. The "Fails open whenever supply pressure is high" choice has the failure behaviour backwards.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional utility wants a meter for a pipe that runs full and has no moving parts. It would measure the voltage made by water moving through a magnetic field. The meter type is:
choices: A nutating disc meter, which needs low flows
A compound meter, which has two chambers
A magnetic meter, which needs a full pipe
A turbine meter, which needs a spinning rotor
finalAssessment.explanation: A magnetic meter has no moving parts but needs a full pipe. The "A nutating disc meter, which needs low flows" choice is a positive displacement design with a moving disc. The "A compound meter, which has two chambers" choice combines low-flow and high-flow measuring chambers. The "A turbine meter, which needs a spinning rotor" choice relies on a rotor.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional contractor leaves a hose in a bucket of soapy water with the other end open on a yard hydrant meter. The link between the drinking water and the bucket is:
choices: A containment device, since it sits at the meter line
A cross-connection, since a path to a contaminant exists
A pressure zone, since it is fed from its own source
An air gap, since the hose end is open to the air
finalAssessment.explanation: A hose in a bucket gives a path for backflow, which makes it a cross-connection. The "A containment device, since it sits at the meter line" choice confuses a hazard with a protective device. The "A pressure zone, since it is fed from its own source" choice confuses plumbing with system zoning. The "An air gap, since the hose end is open to the air" choice would need a true open space above the water level.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional tank at Willow Mill holds 450,000 gal, and on average 180,000 gal passes through it each day. Treat water age as volume divided by daily flow. The approximate water age, in days, is:
choices: 0.40 days
60 days
2.5 days
finalAssessment.explanation: Water age = 450,000 / 180,000 = 2.5 days. The "0.40 days" choice inverted the ratio. The "60 days" choice converted to hours but kept the unit days. The "270,000 days" choice subtracted instead of dividing.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional customer reports low pressure, and a neighbour says hers is normal. The best first thought is that the problem is probably:
choices: A main break that has cut pressure across the zone
A tank that has overflowed at the top of its range
Inside that building or its service, such as a curb stop
A PRV failure that has hit the whole pressure zone
finalAssessment.explanation: When one house is low and the neighbour is normal, the cause is likely local, so check the service and plumbing. The "A main break that has cut pressure across the zone" choice would affect many customers. The "A tank that has overflowed at the top of its range" choice would not lower pressure. The "A PRV failure that has hit the whole pressure zone" choice would also affect many.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional sample siting plan picks locations for coliform sampling. The best plan includes:
choices: Sites that are easy to reach, near the plant and the main office
One convenient tap that is sampled repeatedly each period
Just the newest mains, where the residual is fresh
Representative points, with dead ends and weak-residual areas
finalAssessment.explanation: A siting plan should represent the whole system, including places with the highest risk of trouble. The "Sites that are easy to reach, near the plant and the main office" choice gives a rosy picture. The "One convenient tap that is sampled repeatedly each period" choice hides spatial differences. The "Just the newest mains, where the residual is fresh" choice leaves out older mains.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional operator asks why continuing education is usually required for certification renewal. The best answer is that it:
choices: Keeps operators current on rules, equipment and safety
Replaces the need for an exam at the entry level
Guarantees a pay increase at the next review
Awards contact hours for any course
finalAssessment.explanation: Continuing education keeps knowledge current, and the certifying agency sets the hours. The "Replaces the need for an exam at the entry level" choice mixes up entry exams with renewal. The "Guarantees a pay increase at the next review" choice is not a purpose. The "Awards contact hours for any course" choice is incorrect, since agencies decide what counts.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional steady residual point suddenly reads zero. The best next step is to:
choices: Assume the line is safe and log nothing further
Repeat the test, check the instrument and report it
Flush the whole zone before telling the supervisor
Raise the plant dose on your own
finalAssessment.explanation: A zero reading may be an instrument problem or a real event, so confirm it and report. The "Assume the line is safe and log nothing further" choice skips a possible signal. The "Flush the whole zone before telling the supervisor" choice acts before checking. The "Raise the plant dose on your own" choice changes the plant without authority.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional tank at Pine Hollow has a water surface at elevation 812 ft. A valley customer's service is at elevation 655 ft. Use 0.433 psi per foot of water and 2.31 ft per psi. Ignoring friction, the static pressure at the customer, to one decimal place, is:
choices: 68.0 psi
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Static head is the elevation difference, 812 - 655 = 157 ft, and 157 x 0.433 = 67.98, or 68.0 psi. The "351.6 psi" choice used the tank elevation alone instead of the difference. The "362.7 psi" choice multiplied by 2.31 feet per psi instead of dividing. The "283.6 psi" choice used the customer's elevation alone.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional elevated tank level falls from 104 ft to 88 ft above a gauge during the evening peak. Use 0.433 psi per foot of water. The drop in static pressure at that gauge, to one decimal place, is:
choices: 6.9 psi
37.0 psi
45.0 psi
38.1 psi
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: The change in head is 104 - 88 = 16 ft, and 16 x 0.433 = 6.93, or 6.9 psi. The "37.0 psi" choice multiplied the drop by 2.31 instead of dividing. The "45.0 psi" choice converted the starting level instead of the change. The "38.1 psi" choice converted the ending level instead of the change.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional utility covers and screens its tanks and fits locking hatches mainly so that:
choices: Water level can no longer change with the demand cycle
Water age drops to zero in the tank
Pumps stop needing to start during the evening peak
Outside material stays out, and the tank can be cleaned
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Covers and locked, accessible hatches protect stored water and let crews inspect and clean it. The "Water level can no longer change with the demand cycle" choice is wrong because level still follows demand. The "Water age drops to zero in the tank" choice overstates the effect, since water still sits in the tank. The "Pumps stop needing to start during the evening peak" choice confuses tank cover with the equalising role of storage.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional electrician proposes using a customer's copper water service as the ground for new house wiring. The better answer for the operator is that the practice:
choices: Is fine because metal pipe is such a good conductor
Is unsafe and speeds corrosion, so it is not a ground
Is acceptable if the meter is also bonded across
Helps the cathodic protection system do its work
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Current on a water service can speed corrosion and endanger anyone who cuts into the line, so it must not serve as the electrical ground. The "Is fine because metal pipe is such a good conductor" choice treats conductivity as approval. The "Is acceptable if the meter is also bonded across" choice mixes in meter bonding, which maintains continuity and does not approve grounding use. The "Helps the cathodic protection system do its work" choice confuses stray current with controlled cathodic protection.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional town hopes to improve its ISO fire-protection grading and its pipe network redundancy. The step that helps both is to:
choices: Replace gate valves with a single butterfly valve at the plant
Interconnect dead-end mains into loops and add fire flow
Lower the tank level so more water is stored in the pipes
Remove hydrants from the low-use streets nearby
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Loops and adequate fire flow raise redundancy and improve the water-supply part of the grade. The "Replace gate valves with a single butterfly valve at the plant" choice is valve housekeeping that does not change supply or layout. The "Lower the tank level so more water is stored in the pipes" choice reduces stored water and pressure. The "Remove hydrants from the low-use streets nearby" choice weakens fire protection.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional 12 in main runs 2,000 ft. Use 3.1416 for pi and 7.48 gal per ft3. The volume of water in the main, to the nearest gallon, is:
choices: 210 gal
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Area = 3.1416 x 1 x 1 / 4 = 0.7854 ft2; volume = 0.7854 x 2,000 = 1,570.8 ft3; gallons = 1,570.8 x 7.48 = 11,750. The "46,998 gal" choice forgot to divide the area by 4. The "1,571 gal" choice stayed in cubic feet. The "210 gal" choice divided by 7.48.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional tank needs 36,000 gal to refill. Its pump adds 400 gpm while customer demand removes 250 gpm from the system. Assuming those rates stay steady, the time to refill, in hours, is:
choices: 4.0 hours
1.5 hours
0.9 hours
2.4 hours
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: The net inflow is 400 - 250 = 150 gpm; time = 36,000 / 150 = 240 min = 4.0 hours. The "1.5 hours" choice ignored the demand. The "0.9 hours" choice added demand to the pump rate instead of subtracting. The "2.4 hours" choice used the demand rate alone.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional pressure reducing valve feeds a low zone. The downstream setting matters because it:
choices: Controls how high the upstream tank can fill
Decides which way the check valve will close
Sets the pressure customers in the lower zone feel
Is used to throttle flow for a hydrant flow test
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: A PRV holds its downstream setting, so that setting is the pressure delivered to the lower zone. The "Controls how high the upstream tank can fill" choice describes an altitude valve. The "Decides which way the check valve will close" choice mixes up a PRV with a check valve. The "Is used to throttle flow for a hydrant flow test" choice treats a PRV as a throttling valve for tests.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional utility starts a flushing program. Its main purpose is to:
choices: Raise the static pressure in the main for a while
Lower the rated flow class of nearby hydrants
Test the strength of the pipe wall by pressure
Clear sediment and old water and restore residual
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Flushing replaces old water and clears sediment, with a plan for where the water drains. The "Raise the static pressure in the main for a while" choice is not an effect of opening a hydrant. The "Lower the rated flow class of nearby hydrants" choice confuses flushing with flow testing and has no effect on hydrant class. The "Test the strength of the pipe wall by pressure" choice is not a purpose of flushing.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional utility puts an isolation valve on each hydrant lateral. The purpose is to:
choices: Keep the hydrant barrel from draining after it is used
Isolate one hydrant for repair, keeping the main in service
Restrain the hydrant against thrust from pressure
Throttle fire flow during a hydrant flow test
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: A lateral valve lets the utility repair or replace a hydrant while customers stay in service. The "Keep the hydrant barrel from draining after it is used" choice describes the drain port. The "Restrain the hydrant against thrust from pressure" choice describes thrust blocks or restraints. The "Throttle fire flow during a hydrant flow test" choice misuses an isolation valve, which should be run open or closed.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional leak at Pike Hollow runs at 1.8 gpm for 45 days. Use 1,440 min per day. The total volume lost, in gallons, is:
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Minutes = 1,440 x 45 = 64,800; loss = 1.8 x 64,800 = 116,640 gal. The "1,944 gal" choice used 24 hours instead of 1,440 minutes. The "2,592 gal" choice counted a single day. The "872,467 gal" choice multiplied by 7.48 even though the rate is already in gallons.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional utility needs protection at an irrigation system with no downstream pump and a risk of backsiphonage only. Of these, the device that fits that duty is:
choices: A pressure vacuum breaker
A strainer on the meter inlet
A single check with no testing
A plain gate valve
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: A pressure vacuum breaker suits backsiphonage where no backpressure can occur. The "A strainer on the meter inlet" choice filters debris but gives no backflow protection. The "A single check with no testing" choice gives weak protection and no way to confirm it works. The "A plain gate valve" choice stops flow in either direction but is not a backflow device.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional utility puts one device at a customer's meter and another at a fixture inside. The one at the meter that protects the whole system from the customer is called:
choices: Containment, which protects the system from that site
Isolation, which protects a single fixture inside
Equalising, which balances tank levels in the zone
Exercising, which operates the valve on a schedule
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Containment at the meter or property line protects the system, while isolation protects the fixture. The "Isolation, which protects a single fixture inside" choice names the other approach. The "Equalising, which balances tank levels in the zone" choice is a storage term. The "Exercising, which operates the valve on a schedule" choice is a valve maintenance term.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional utility tests its large commercial meters more often than its small residential meters. The reason is that large meters:
choices: Lose accuracy faster than any other meter
Are made from different pipe materials
Pass more volume, so a small error costs more
Are impossible to test after installation
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: More water passes through a large meter, so an error costs more revenue. The "Lose accuracy faster than any other meter" choice is a guess, since accuracy depends on the design and wear. The "Are made from different pipe materials" choice is unrelated to testing. The "Are impossible to test after installation" choice is false, since meters can be tested in place or removed.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional backflow assembly passed its test last year, and the owner asks why it must be tested again. The best reason is that:
choices: The assembly changes its hazard rating over time
Springs, seats and checks can wear or foul unseen
The water in the main changes its source each year
A tester must be paid to keep the assembly valid
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Mechanical parts can fail silently, so periodic tests by a qualified tester confirm they work. The "The assembly changes its hazard rating over time" choice mixes up hazard rating with device condition. The "The water in the main changes its source each year" choice is not a reason for testing. The "A tester must be paid to keep the assembly valid" choice misreads the purpose.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional dead-end main reads 1.80 mg/L free chlorine leaving the plant and 0.45 mg/L at the end. The percent of residual lost along the way, to the nearest whole percent, is:
choices: 25 percent
300 percent
75 percent
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Loss = (1.80 - 0.45) / 1.80 x 100 = 75 percent. The "25 percent" choice reported the share that remains. The "300 percent" choice divided the loss by the end value instead of the starting value. The "1.35 mg/L" choice gave the loss in mg/L, not a percent.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional caller reports an odd taste in cold water only. The best record includes:
choices: Just the caller's name and a note to call back
A guess about who caused the problem and when
Date, address, contact, complaint, hot or cold, findings
The caller's opinion about the utility's water rates
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: A complete record lets the utility see patterns. The "Just the caller's name and a note to call back" choice leaves out the details. The "A guess about who caused the problem and when" choice records speculation. The "The caller's opinion about the utility's water rates" choice records opinion.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional utility prepares a service-line inventory. The purpose is to:
choices: Set the target pressure for each pressure zone
Test the strength of each service pipe by pressure
Record the date each hydrant was last painted
Show which lines are lead, galvanized or unknown
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: An inventory shows where lead may be, so the utility can plan sampling and replacement. The "Set the target pressure for each pressure zone" choice relates to zoning. The "Test the strength of each service pipe by pressure" choice would need a pressure test. The "Record the date each hydrant was last painted" choice is a hydrant record.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional operator works with the regulator after a violation. The best practice is to:
choices: Report problems early, keep records and ask when unsure
Wait to see if the problem goes away on its own
Speak about health effects without confirming them
Rely on memory when the records are missing or late
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Early, honest reporting with records builds trust. The "Wait to see if the problem goes away on its own" choice delays a needed report. The "Speak about health effects without confirming them" choice speculates on health. The "Rely on memory when the records are missing or late" choice weakens credibility.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional zone has oversized mains and low use. Water age is most likely to:
choices: Fall, because larger pipes flush themselves
Rise, because water stays longer in the pipes
Stay constant, because tanks set it
Drop to zero, because the residual is high
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Oversized mains with low use hold water longer, so age rises. The "Fall, because larger pipes flush themselves" choice reverses the effect. The "Stay constant, because tanks set it" choice ignores local conditions. The "Drop to zero, because the residual is high" choice confuses a residual with age.
